name: Ran, or verified?
note: Executing AI code on the example you were handed is the weakest possible evidence. Pick the move that turns 'it ran' into 'it's verified'.

items.prompt: The candidate runs the AI code on the provided example; it returns the right answer. They declare it 'verified'. Accurate?
candidates: No — one happy-path run is the case most likely to pass; verification means running the preregistered boundary and invariant cases, not the example you were handed
Yes — correct output is correct output
No — you must always hit 100% line coverage first
Yes, as long as it ran without throwing an exception
items.correct: No — one happy-path run is the case most likely to pass; verification means running the preregistered boundary and invariant cases, not the example you were handed
items.explanation: A single example run is a demo, not verification. Verification is passing the gate you committed before seeing the code — boundaries, invariants, adversarial inputs.
items.principle: Running the example proves the least; running the gate proves the point.

items.prompt: The code fails a boundary test. The candidate re-prompts 'it's broken, please fix.' Better move?
candidates: Feed the specific failure: 'fails on empty input — returns None, should return []; fix that without changing the non-empty behavior' — the verification result is the best debugging prompt
'It's broken, please fix' — let the AI rediscover the problem on its own
Regenerate from scratch with the same original prompt
Accept it; boundary failures are edge cases that rarely matter
items.correct: Feed the specific failure: 'fails on empty input — returns None, should return []; fix that without changing the non-empty behavior' — the verification result is the best debugging prompt
items.explanation: A precise failure description turns the AI into a targeted debugger; a vague one is prompt-roulette. The loop is review → run → confirm, fed by exactly what the gate reported.
items.principle: Debug the AI with the verification result, not with 'it's broken.'

items.prompt: Two candidates both reach green tests. One wrote the tests from the spec before prompting; the other after seeing the code. Same confidence?
candidates: No — green on preregistered tests verifies against an independent standard; green on post-hoc tests can just confirm whatever the code already did
Yes — green is green regardless of when the tests were written
No — the second candidate is always the more thorough one
Yes, as long as both suites have the same number of tests
items.correct: No — green on preregistered tests verifies against an independent standard; green on post-hoc tests can just confirm whatever the code already did
items.explanation: Verification strength depends on the independence of the standard from the code. Preregistration (Ch 3) is what makes 'the tests pass' a claim about correctness rather than a mirror of the implementation.
items.principle: Green means something only when the test couldn't have been shaped by the code.
